title: AIDLC adoption profile
description: The machine-readable output of /aidlc:adopt — an evidence-backed profile of an existing workspace, written to .aidlc/adoption/profile.json. This file is the CONTRACT the later adoption stories read (config writing, gate derivation, convention adoption, drift detection); it is not itself configuration and nothing in the pipeline is steered by it until a human has approved a step that reads it. Every derived fact is a `fact` object carrying evidence and confidence, or is recorded absent/unknown — a value without evidence is a schema violation, not a guess. See docs/brownfield-adoption.md (ADOPT-2) and the aidlc:adopt skill.

profileVersion.description: Contract version. Bump only for a BREAKING change (a field removed, renamed, or given new semantics); additive blocks do not bump it, which is why every object here allows additional properties. A consumer that does not recognise the version must say so and stop rather than read the file optimistically.

scan.description: Provenance and cost of this scan. A profile without it cannot be compared against a later one, so drift detection depends on it.

scannedAt.description: UTC ISO-8601 timestamp of the scan.

aidlcVersion.description: Version of the aidlc plugin that produced this profile.

depth.description: How much the scan was allowed to look at. quick = manifests, IDE/VCS metadata and top-level config only (the 10-minute pass; useful alone). standard = adds config parsing, CI files and package/workspace enumeration. deep = adds bounded source sampling for the runtime facts that only source evidences. Depth is the cost dial, not a quality claim: a quick scan records more `unknown`, never a guess.

commit.description: Control-plane HEAD (or the scanned root's HEAD) at scan time. Re-running against the same commit must produce the same profile — that is what makes adoption idempotent.

controlPlane.description: Where AIDLC's control plane resolved to, and why. Never a product repo by default.

path.description: Absolute path of the control-plane folder.

resolvedFrom.description: code-workspace-file: the folder holding the *.code-workspace file (preferred — it holds regardless of which folder the IDE hands the session as cwd). opened-folder: no workspace file, so the session's cwd. user: the user overrode the resolution.

isWorkspaceRoot.description: Whether the control-plane folder is itself one of the workspace roots. False means the session cannot read it unless it is added; adopt offers to add it.

alreadyAdopted.description: True when an aidlc.config.json already exists here — the run is a re-adoption/drift scan, not a first contact.

budget.description: What the scan actually cost. Stated in the report so a reader knows the difference between 'clean' and 'not looked at'.

caps.description: The limits this depth applied, so 'we stopped here' is distinguishable from 'there was nothing more'.

maxAdrCandidates.description: Cap on how many retroactive-ADR candidates the scan proposes (adrCandidates[] with status=propose). Ranked by reversibility cost, so the cap drops the cheapest-to-change decisions first. Recorded here rather than assumed so a reader can tell a short list from a truncated one.

maxDebtFindings.description: Cap on debtFindings[]. Ranked by severity, so the cap drops hygiene before it drops an unreviewed auth path. Twenty is already more than most teams will triage in one sitting; the point of recording the cap is that a reader can tell a short list from a truncated one.

hitCap.description: True if a cap terminated the scan early. When true the report must say which cap and what was left unread.

skipped.description: Everything deliberately not looked at. An empty array is a claim of full coverage — only make it when true.

reason.description: lfs-pointer: the file is an LFS stub, so reading it would profile the pointer, not the content. env-file / pii-suspect: excluded by the safety contract, not by cost.

sampling.description: Set when a root was too large to read fully. Absent/applied=false means no sampling was needed.

strategy.description: How the sample was chosen, e.g. 'all manifests + entry points + the 200 largest source files by directory breadth'.

coveragePercent.description: Share of in-scope source files actually inspected. Reported verbatim; never rounded up to imply completeness.

writes.description: The read-only guarantee, recorded rather than asserted. paths[] must contain ONLY files under .aidlc/adoption/.

sessionOnly.description: True when the workspace was not writable and the report was printed to the session instead of written. paths[] is then empty.

network.description: Adopt makes no network calls to analyse code and sends no source anywhere. Host-API lookups (branch policy, required checks) are the only outbound calls it may make, are optional, and each is recorded here.

sourceTransmitted.description: Always false. Present so a reviewer can verify the guarantee from the artifact.

hostApiCalls.description: Read-only host API calls made, e.g. 'gh api repos/:owner/:repo/branches/main/protection'. Empty when offline or declined.

offline.description: True when outbound calls failed or were unavailable. The checks that depended on them are then recorded unknown, and the scan still completes.

workspace.description: The workspace is the unit of adoption — not the repo. A repo is a routing target inside it.

shape.description: How the IDE workspace is arranged. single-root: one folder, one repo. nested-multi-repo: one opened folder with repos as subfolders. multi-root: a *.code-workspace folders[] list whose entries may live anywhere, including other drives.

codeWorkspaceFile.description: Absolute path of the *.code-workspace file, or status absent when there is none. Absent is normal and must not degrade the scan — JetBrains, a plain terminal and CI have no such file, and the folder scan is then the only signal.

topology.description: AIDLC's topology classification for the workspace. single-app: one repo, one deliverable. monorepo: one git repo, many independently-owned packages. poly: many git repos. The deciding signal goes in evidence — a classification with no named signal is a guess.

roots.description: Every folder the workspace exposes, classified. Only product-repo and monorepo entries are candidates for a repos[] entry in config; the rest are recorded so the report can explain why they were excluded.

surfaces.description: The honest-degradation table: every surface the scan detected, and whether the INSTALLED plugins actually cover it. Drives the report's supported/partial/unsupported table and the capability gaps below. Never claim a capability the installed plugins do not provide.

detected.description: What is actually in use, e.g. 'Django 5 + Celery', 'GitHub Issues', 'Perforce'.

root.description: Root name this applies to; omit for workspace-wide surfaces.

providedBy.description: The installed plugin/skill that covers it, when support is supported/partial, e.g. 'aidlc-stack-web'.

consequence.description: One line stating what the user loses. Required even when supported (then: what they get). A gap with no stated consequence reads as a footnote instead of a decision.

gaps.description: Capability gaps to be recorded in .aidlc/extensions.json so /aidlc:scaffold-skill and /aidlc:promote can act on them later. Derived from surfaces[] where support is partial or unsupported. Writing these is an approved step, not part of the read-only scan.

kind.description: What would close the gap. skill/agent/plugin/adapter: something AIDLC builds, and the entry is a genuine extension candidate. project-action: something only the PROJECT can close (run git init on a zip drop, adopt a tracker, upgrade an EOL runtime) — recorded so an unsupported surface is never left with no named next step, but never proposed to /aidlc:scaffold-skill.

workaround.description: What the project uses until then, e.g. 'markdown backlog as the tracker adapter'.

debtFindings.description:
What the scan found that is WORK rather than a fact about the project — the debt-backlog proposals of ADOPT-11. Ordered by severity, HIGHEST FIRST, and capped by scan.budget.caps.maxDebtFindings, for the same reason adrCandidates is ranked: a capped unranked list drops exactly the findings worth tracking. Seeding a backlog from these is a separate opt-in step (/aidlc:adopt-backlog) which dedupes against the tracker and proposes every item before creating it; the scan writes nothing to any tracker.

A finding is an observation with evidence, not a remedy. It carries no fix, patch or diff: how to close the debt is normal pipeline work, decided when the item is run, and a scan that also prescribed the solution would be guessing about code it only sampled.

The `sensitive` flag is the one field with teeth. A tracker item may be a PUBLIC GitHub issue, so a finding that names where an unfixed credential or a PII fixture lives would turn adoption into a disclosure. Sensitive findings therefore carry a trackerSafeTitle and no paths, and point the reader at the adoption report — which stays in the repo.

drift.description:
Present only on a RE-ADOPTION: the comparison between what a previous scan recorded, what the code shows now, and what the config currently says. Adoption is not a one-shot event — codebases drift from their recorded profile, and a re-scan whose only output was a fresh full profile would leave a reader to diff two large JSON files by eye.

The comparison is deliberately three-way, because two of the three differences must be treated in opposite ways. Code that moved since the last scan is drift to propose. A config value that no longer matches the code is drift to propose. A config value that differs from what the last apply WROTE is a human's deliberate edit — intent the scan cannot see and must never offer to overwrite. Collapsing the third case into the first is how a re-adoption quietly reverts a hand-tuned gate, with a diff that looks like routine convergence.

baseline.description: What this scan compared itself against. The previous profile.json is the preferred baseline, which is why both adoption artifacts are meant to be git-tracked — an untracked profile leaves a re-scan with nothing to diff.

kind.description: previous-profile: a prior .aidlc/adoption/profile.json was read before being overwritten — the full baseline. config-only: no previous profile survived, so only the config's recorded values could be compared, and facts the config does not carry are unknown-not-unchanged. none: first adoption, or no baseline was readable — then changes[] MUST be empty, because reporting a whole project as 'new drift' on first contact is noise that teaches people to skip the section.

path.description: Where the baseline came from, e.g. '.aidlc/adoption/profile.json' or '.claude/aidlc.config.json'.

commit.description: The commit the baseline was taken at. Equal to scan.commit means the code has not moved, so any change recorded here comes from config or from a change in the scan itself.

depth.description: The baseline scan's depth. A different depth explains most apparent movement: facts the earlier run never sampled come back known now, which is new KNOWLEDGE, not new drift. This enum must stay identical to scan.depth — the validator's test suite checks both against each other.

appliedAt.description: From the config's adoption.appliedAt — when the baseline profile was last applied. A config value that changed after this timestamp was changed by a human.

depthChanged.description: True when this scan's depth differs from the baseline's. Required to be true when they differ, because it changes how the whole section reads: a quick→deep re-scan turns dozens of `unknown`s into facts, and presenting those as project drift buries the two or three changes that really are.

comparedAgainstConfig.description: Whether the current .claude/aidlc.config.json was read as the third leg of the comparison. False means config drift and human edits could not be distinguished, which must be said rather than silently reported as no drift.

unmanaged.description: Surfaces the config's adoption.unmanaged deliberately excluded (a repo or package the team is not piloting on). Echoed here so this run reports them once as 'unmanaged by choice' instead of re-proposing them every scan — the difference between 'not adopted' and 'missed'.

changes.description: One entry per difference found. An empty array is the good outcome and the observable proof of idempotency: a re-scan at the same commit and depth must produce none.

adrCandidates.description:
Decisions already embedded in the code that have no ADR recording them — the retroactive-ADR proposals of ADOPT-10. On a brownfield project docs/adr/ is empty while the decisions themselves are everywhere in the code, which starves /aidlc:do and the architect of the one thing they cannot re-derive. Ordered by reversibility cost, HIGHEST FIRST: the cap keeps the decisions that would be expensive to undo and drops the cheap ones. Writing an ADR from a candidate is a separate approved step (/aidlc:adopt-adr) with per-ADR approval — this array proposes, and the scan writes nothing to docs/adr/.

A candidate records WHAT was decided and the code that proves it. It must not record WHY: the reason lives in a conversation the scan never saw, and an invented rationale in an accepted ADR is worse than an empty one because every later reader treats it as history. The forbidden-field rule below is what makes that mechanical rather than aspirational.

safety.description: What the scan found that must be handled rather than reported plainly. Locations and shapes only — never values.

envFiles.description: Env files by PATH ONLY. Contents are never read and variable names appear here only when pipeline.envFileAccess permits it and the env-guard hook allowed the read.

contentsRead.description: False unless pipeline.envFileAccess is 'ask' AND the user approved the read. When false, variableNames must be absent.

variableNames.description: Variable NAMES only, never values. Present only when contentsRead is true.

gitTracked.description: True is a finding in itself — a tracked env file is a committed-secret risk regardless of its current content.

secretFindings.description: Suspected secrets, redacted. Location and type only — the value is never written here, into the report, into an item, or into a commit.

type.description: Kind of credential, e.g. 'AWS access key id', 'private key block', 'connection string with password'.

redacted.description: Always true. The field exists so its absence fails validation rather than passing silently.

piiSuspects.description: Fixture/seed files that look like they carry personal data. Flagged for human review and excluded from any content quoted into the report.

signal.description: Why it looks like PII, e.g. 'columns email, phone, dob in seed/customers.csv'. Never a sample row.

support.description: supported: an installed plugin covers it end to end. partial: the language-agnostic core applies but the stack/tracker specifics do not. unsupported: nothing covers it — say so and record the gap. unknown: not established.

evidence.description: One citation. Evidence is what separates a derived fact from a guess, so every known and every absent fact carries at least one.

kind.description: path: a file (with `line`, a path:line citation). command: a command and its output. absence: a stated search that found nothing — the evidence for an `absent` fact. user: the user told us, in answer to a low-confidence question.

path.description: Repo-relative where a root is implied, otherwise absolute.

excerpt.description: At most one short verbatim line, for legibility. Never taken from an env file, a secret finding or a PII-suspect file, and never a substitute for the path:line citation.

output.description: Trimmed command output. Truncate long output and say so; do not paste a suite log.

note.description: For kind=absence, what was searched and came back empty, e.g. 'no test script in package.json, no pytest.ini/tox.ini, no tests/ or **/*.test.* files'.

fact.description: One derived fact. The three statuses are deliberately distinct: `known` (established, with evidence), `absent` (the thing provably is not there — a gate that does not exist, a remote that is not configured), and `unknown` (could not be established). Collapsing absent into unknown loses a coverage hole; collapsing unknown into a default value is how a wrong inference reaches CLAUDE.md and steers every later run.

value.description: The derived value. Required when status is known; meaningless otherwise.

confidence.description: high: a manifest/config/command states it outright. medium: converging indirect signals. low: one weak signal — a low-confidence fact is presented to the user as a QUESTION, never as a proposed value.

reason.description: Why the fact could not be established. Required when status is unknown; it is what makes the gap actionable instead of invisible.

commandFact.description: A fact whose value is a runnable command — an entry point the project already has. status=absent means the project genuinely has no such command, which is a coverage hole to report, not a value to invent.

cmd.description: Verbatim, as the project runs it, e.g. 'pnpm -w test', 'mvn -pl api verify', 'uv run pytest'.

cwd.description: Directory to run it from, relative to the root. Omit for the root itself.

source.description: Where it came from, e.g. 'package.json scripts.test', 'Makefile target test', 'tox.ini envlist'.

environmentDependent.description: True when it needs services (compose, testcontainers, a live DB). A failure must then be diagnosed as 'environment unavailable', not 'code broken'.

gate.description: One step in a root's verification sequence. `present` carries the command the project already runs; `absent` carries no command and is a stated coverage hole. There is no third state — a gate invented from an AIDLC default is neither, and is what this shape exists to prevent.

name.description: Short stable id — lint, typecheck, test, format, build, boundaries, migrate-check, or a project-specific one.

status.description: present: the project has this gate. absent: it could have it and does not — a coverage hole the run reports every time. not-applicable: the stack has no such step (no build for a Django service; Go type-checks during `go build`), so it is neither run nor reported as a hole.

cmd.description: Verbatim, as the project runs it. Required when status=present, forbidden when absent.

cwd.description: Directory to run it from, relative to the root. Omit for the root itself.

source.description: Where it came from — 'package.json scripts.test', 'Makefile target lint', 'tox.ini envlist', 'turbo.json tasks.test', '.pre-commit-config.yaml'.

required.description: Whether a failure blocks the item. An absent gate is required=false by construction — it cannot block, and pretending otherwise would make a missing gate look green.

scope.description: What the gate runs over per item. repo: the whole root. package: one package (monorepo). affected: an affected-graph runner's affected set (Nx/Turbo) — the cheap correct default where one exists. changed-paths: a subset derived from the diff, for a suite too slow to run whole.

package.description: The package this gate belongs to, when scope=package.

timeoutMinutes.description: Only when the PROJECT states one (a CI job timeout). Never a number you made up — an unmeasured suite duration is unknown, and the scoping decision is then made explicitly rather than on a fabricated figure.

environmentDependent.description: True when the gate needs services — Docker Compose, testcontainers, a live DB, a message broker. This is what lets a failure be diagnosed as 'environment unavailable' rather than 'code broken', which is the difference between a useful run report and a misleading one.

services.description: The services it needs, e.g. ['postgres', 'redis']. Present when environmentDependent is true.

providedByHook.description: Set when a pre-existing hook manager already runs this gate at commit time (husky, pre-commit, lefthook). The AIDLC pre-commit layer must NOT duplicate it.

alsoInCi.description: Whether CI runs the same gate. A gate in CI but not locally (or vice versa) is a parity gap worth naming.

detected.description: One detected thing (language, package manager, framework, CI system, migration tool) with the paths that carry it. A polyglot repo lists ALL of them, never just the dominant one.

version.description: As declared by the project, e.g. '3.12' from pyproject requires-python. Never inferred from what is installed on this machine.

paths.description: Where it lives. Load-bearing for a polyglot repo: per-path gates and per-path standards depend on it.

adrCandidate.description: One irreversible decision the code already embodies, proposed as a retroactive ADR. `propose` means no ADR records it yet; `already-recorded` means one does and it is listed here anyway, so a re-run's silence is legible as 'checked and covered' rather than 'never looked'.

decisionKind.description: The decision's topic, from a closed list so de-duplication against already-recorded ADRs is mechanical rather than a judgement call on titles. Unique per profile: two candidates for the same topic means one decision would get two ADRs.

title.description: The decision as a STATEMENT, in the ADR template's voice — 'Store tenant data in one shared Postgres schema keyed by tenant_id', not 'Database choice'. It becomes the ADR's H1.

status.description: propose: no ADR covers this decision — a candidate for /aidlc:adopt-adr. already-recorded: docs/adr/ (or a linked external doc) already records it, so it is NOT proposed again. Recording it rather than dropping it is what makes re-adoption's no-new-ADRs outcome verifiable.

existingAdr.description: Path or URL of the ADR/doc that already records this decision. Required when status=already-recorded, forbidden when status=propose.

reversibilityCost.description: What undoing this decision would cost — the ranking key, since an ADR earns its page by being hard to reverse. high: a data model, tenancy model or public contract that consumers depend on. medium: a framework or deployment shape. low: a tooling choice a day's work replaces.

root.description: The root whose code evidences it; omit for a workspace-wide decision.

decidedAt.description: When the decision was made, where history establishes it (the commit that introduced the pattern). status=unknown is the common and correct answer on a squashed or shallow history — the ADR's Date then reads `unknown`, never a plausible guess.

consequencesObserved.description: Consequences VISIBLE IN THE CODE — 'every query must filter by tenant_id, and 3 repositories do it by hand'. Observation, not judgement: what the code shows, not whether it was wise.

rationale.description: FORBIDDEN, along with its four synonyms below. The scan can see WHAT was decided and never WHY — the why lives in a conversation it did not witness. The rendered ADR marks `## Rationale` and `## Alternatives considered` as *not recorded — confirm with the team*; a plausible sentence here becomes permanent history nobody authored and everybody cites. Each spelling is forbidden individually rather than by `additionalProperties: false`, because this object stays additive (a new field must not require a profileVersion bump) — so the ban has to name what it bans. validate-profile.mjs enforces the same five.

alternatives.description: FORBIDDEN — see `rationale`. The scan cannot know what was rejected, and listing the obvious alternatives as though they had been weighed is the same invention in a different section.

debtFinding.description: One piece of debt the scan can evidence — an absent gate, an untested critical path, an end-of-life runtime, a TODO cluster, a sensitive path with no review history, documentation that contradicts the code. It is a candidate work item, not a work item: /aidlc:adopt-backlog dedupes it against the tracker, writes the acceptance criteria and proposes it before anything is created.

kind.description: absent-gate: a verification step the project does not have (must name the gate). untested-critical-path: an auth/billing/tenant-isolation path with no test covering it. eol-dependency: a declared runtime or dependency past end of life — the evidence is the DECLARATION in the repo, and the EOL judgement must be stated as needing confirmation, because this scan makes no network calls and cannot check a release calendar. todo-cluster: a concentration of TODO/FIXME/HACK markers dense enough to be a backlog item rather than a comment. unreviewed-sensitive-path: a security-review path whose history shows no review. docs-drift: documentation contradicted by the code it describes. committed-secret / pii-in-fixtures: derived from safety findings, and always sensitive. cross-platform-hazard: mixed line endings with no .gitattributes, a case-colliding pair of paths, an OS-specific lockfile. ungated-integration: a repo whose PRs merge with no required check, where the host API actually answered.

title.description: The work as an OUTCOME, in the voice of a work item — 'Add a typecheck gate to the payments service', not 'No typecheck'. It becomes the item's title, and a title that only names the symptom produces an item nobody can tell is finished.

severity.description: The ranking key, so the cap drops the cheapest findings rather than an arbitrary tail. high: it can cause customer-visible or security-relevant harm (an unreviewed auth path, a committed secret, no tests around billing). medium: it degrades the pipeline's ability to verify (an absent gate, an EOL runtime). low: hygiene.

root.description: The root this belongs to, by name; omit for a workspace-wide finding. It resolves to the item's `repo`.

package.description: The package inside a monorepo root, when the finding is package-scoped. It resolves to the item's `package`.

gate.description: Which gate is missing. REQUIRED when kind is absent-gate, and it must name a gate the root actually records as status=absent — otherwise the finding proposes work for a gate the project already has, which is how a debt backlog loses its credibility on the first item somebody checks.

paths.description: Where the debt lives, so the item is actionable. Forbidden when `sensitive` is true — see trackerSafeTitle.

suggestedType.description: The item type this would become. A finding whose remedy is genuinely unclear is a spike, not a story with invented acceptance criteria.

suggestedSize.description: Rough size, so the created item is never a bare title. XL means it should be decomposed before it is created.

sensitive.description: True when naming the finding's location would itself disclose something — a credential still in history, a fixture full of personal data, an exploitable path with no review. A tracker item may be a PUBLIC issue, and 'AWS key at scripts/deploy.sh:14 in commit 9ac31be' published to the internet turns adoption into an incident. True is REQUIRED for kind committed-secret and pii-in-fixtures.

trackerSafeTitle.description: A title that discloses nothing and points at the adoption report instead — 'Rotate a credential found in git history (details in .aidlc/adoption/report.md)'. Required when `sensitive` is true; it is what /aidlc:adopt-backlog puts on the item, and the specifics stay in the repo where the report lives.

evidence.description: Required, as everywhere else. Note the asymmetry with `paths`: evidence lives in the profile, which is a file in the team's own repo, and it never travels to the tracker item — so a sensitive finding may cite where it looked here while still disclosing nothing outward.

confidence.description: An EOL claim or a docs-drift reading is rarely `high` — say so, and the proposed item then says so too rather than asserting a fact the team may already know to be wrong.

note.description: One line the fields do not carry — most usefully, what still needs confirming. An EOL finding belongs here: 'Ruby 2.7 reached end of life in 2023 — confirm against ruby-lang.org, since this scan makes no network calls.'

fix.description: FORBIDDEN, with `remedy`, `patch`, `diff` and `solution`. The scan sampled the code; it did not design the change. A finding that ships its own remedy invites the item to be closed by applying it unread, and the pipeline's whole point is that a change is planned, implemented, reviewed and verified. State the debt; let /aidlc:run decide the fix.

remedy.description: FORBIDDEN — see `fix`. (`reachable.remedy` and `trust.remedy` are a different thing entirely: they tell the USER how to make a root readable, and are required there.)

driftChange.description: One difference between the baseline, the code and the config. `source` and `action` together are the whole point of the record: they say whose change this was and therefore what may be done about it.

kind.description: What moved. root-added/root-removed cover the VS Code case where a user adds or drops a folder after adoption. adr-superseded: the code no longer matches a decision a recorded ADR describes — reported for a human, never resolved by the scan, because superseding an ADR is a decision and not a detection.

surface.description: The specific thing, named the way config names it — 'repos[].api.pipeline.gates.verify.steps.test', 'packages[].@acme/web', 'git.integrationBranch'. A drift entry a reader cannot locate is a rumour.

root.description: Root name, where the change is root-scoped.

was.description: The baseline value. null where the thing did not exist then.

now.description: The current value. null where it no longer exists. Equal to `was` is not drift and must not be recorded.

source.description: code: the project moved — the ordinary case, and drift worth proposing. config: configuration no longer matches the code (a gate command renamed, a package deleted but still registered). human-edit: the config differs from what the last apply wrote, so somebody changed it deliberately after adoption — INTENT the scan cannot see. scan-depth: explained by this run looking deeper (or less deep) than the baseline, which is a change in knowledge rather than in the project. unknown: the baseline could not establish which, which must be said rather than assumed to be code.

action.description: What the apply step may do. propose: offer the change as a config diff. report-only: state it and stop (an unmanaged surface, an ADR the code has outgrown, a finding whose remedy is not configuration). leave-alone: REQUIRED for source=human-edit — a hand-authored value is never proposed for overwrite, because a diff that reverts a deliberate edit looks exactly like routine convergence and is the one drift outcome nobody would catch in review.

evidence.description: Required when source=code: the citation proving the project actually moved. A config or human-edit difference is evidenced by the two values themselves.

note.description: One line a reader needs that the fields do not carry.

saasProfile.description: The runtime constraints that change how code must be WRITTEN, which are not in the stack list. For a live SaaS, 'TypeScript + Postgres' says far less about a safe change than 'shared-schema multi-tenant, migrations run against live data, releases ride feature flags, and the OpenAPI file is a public contract'. Every field is a fact, so an unevidenced constraint is `unknown` — and `unknown` here means the agent briefs stay silent rather than asserting a constraint that may not exist. Most of these need `depth: deep` (they are evidenced in source, not manifests); a quick scan is expected to leave the block sparse.

tenancy.description: How tenants are isolated — the single most constraining runtime fact. shared-schema: one schema, rows keyed by a tenant column (every query must filter; a missing filter is a cross-tenant data leak). schema-per-tenant / database-per-tenant: isolation is structural, but migrations must fan out. single-tenant: one customer per deployment. not-multi-tenant: not a tenanted product at all. Evidence is a tenant column, a schema-switching middleware, or a per-tenant connection resolver — never the marketing copy in the README.

tenantIsolationPaths.description: value: [paths] carrying the isolation mechanism itself (the tenant-scoping middleware, the row-level-security policies, the connection resolver). A change here can leak one customer's data into another's response, so these paths are security-review paths regardless of the configured cadence — they must appear in securityReviewPathSeeds.

authPaths.description: value: [paths] carrying authentication, authorization, SSO, RBAC or session handling. Always security-review paths, for the same reason as tenant isolation — they must appear in securityReviewPathSeeds.

billingPaths.description: value: [paths] carrying billing, subscription, entitlement or metering logic. Revenue-critical: a silent bug here bills the wrong amount, so these join securityReviewPathSeeds too.

featureFlags.description: value: {provider, paths[]} for a flag system in use (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, OpenFeature, or a homegrown table). When known, the implementer brief must state that user-visible changes ship behind a flag — that is the project's release mechanism, and ignoring it puts an unflagged change in front of every customer at merge.

migrations.description: value: {tool, directory} for the migration tool and where its migrations live (Prisma, TypeORM, Alembic, Flyway, Liquibase, EF Core, Rails, Django, golang-migrate). Also recorded in migrationTools[]; repeated here because the SaaS constraint attaches to it.

liveDataConstraint.description: Whether schema changes must be expand/contract with a backfill rather than break-and-fix. `expand-contract` whenever migrations run against live data shared by tenants — then a destructive migration (a dropped or renamed column, a narrowed type, a NOT NULL on an existing column) is a review BLOCKER, not a style note. `not-required` only where the evidence actually supports it (a single-tenant install migrated on upgrade, a pre-launch schema).

apiContracts.description: value: [{kind, path, public}]. These paths ARE the contract-affecting set: a diff touching one marks the item contract-affecting so breaking-change review runs regardless of cadence. `public: true` means external consumers depend on it and a break is a customer-visible incident.

environments.description: value: [{name, kind}] from CI/CD config, deploy manifests or environment definitions — not from a guess about what a team probably has.

deployStrategy.description: How a change reaches production, from CI/CD config. Load-bearing with feature flags: canary or flag-gated delivery is why a change may merge before it is visible.

freezeWindows.description: value: [{when, source}] for deploy freezes or release trains the project declares (a CI schedule guard, a documented change-freeze calendar). Surfaced at integration when a merge would violate one — recorded, never enforced silently.

compliance.description: value: [{regime, signal}]. The SIGNAL must be named (a BAA reference, a PCI SAQ, a data-processing addendum, an audit-evidence directory) — a compliance claim inferred from the word 'secure' in a README is exactly the wrong kind of fact to put in permanent config, since it raises the review cost of every future change.

messaging.description: value: [{name, kind, paths[]}]. Background jobs and event contracts have consumers that a diff can break invisibly — a changed message shape is a contract change without a contract file.
messaging.$comment: The kind enum here is duplicated in validate-profile.mjs as MESSAGING_KINDS and cross-checked by its test suite.

observability.description: value: [{name, paths[]}] for error tracking / metrics / tracing (Sentry, Datadog, OpenTelemetry, Grafana). Recorded because incidents are a legitimate intake source, and because a change that drops instrumentation is a regression nobody's tests catch.

integrations.description: value: [{name, paths[], sandboxEvidence?}] for third-party services and webhooks. Recorded so a change at that seam is reviewed as an integration change; production credentials remain barred by rules/safety.md regardless of what is recorded here.

experimentation.description: value: {provider, paths[]} for A/B testing or analytics-driven rollout, where evidenced.

securityReviewPathSeeds.description: The union of every path above that must trigger security review regardless of the configured cadence — tenant isolation, auth, billing, and paths a named compliance regime governs. This is the array /aidlc:adopt-apply proposes into pipeline.securityReviewPaths (union with what is already there, never a replacement). It is derived, not independent: a path recorded in authPaths, tenantIsolationPaths or billingPaths and missing here is a silently un-reviewed path, which is the failure ADOPT-9's last two criteria exist to prevent.

root.description: One workspace root (a folder the IDE exposes, or a subfolder found by the folder scan), classified and — when it is a product repo or monorepo — profiled.

name.description: Short id: the *.code-workspace `name` override when present, else the folder name. Becomes the repos[] name if this root is adopted.

path.description: As written in the source that declared it (a .code-workspace folders[].path is often relative to that file).

absolutePath.description: Resolved absolute path. The authoritative locator: roots may sit outside the control plane, on another drive, or on a UNC share.

nestedUnderControlPlane.description: Whether this root lives inside the control-plane folder. False disables the .gitignore/gitlink protection as inapplicable (there is no control-plane git index to accidentally stage it into) and requires an absolute repo.path in config.

declaredBy.description: How the root was discovered. Both discovery paths run: a .code-workspace folders[] list AND a scan for <sub>/.git — otherwise a multi-root workspace collapses to a single repo.

classification.description: control-plane: the folder holding the board, the ADRs, aidlc.config.json and the tracked adoption profile. Usually its own git repo and usually NOT a product repo — it is excluded from repos[] by name, so work is never routed to a repo with no code. product-repo: ours, one deliverable, a routing target. monorepo: ours, one git repo with many packages. non-repo: docs/scratch/notes — excluded from repos[]. reference-only: a clone we read but do not change (a vendor SDK, an upstream we track) — never a routing target. already-adopted: carries its own aidlc.config.json. not-cloned: declared but absent on disk — record it, never fabricate a path. Every classification is PROPOSED for confirmation, never assumed.

reachable.description: Whether the running session can actually read this root. Adopt never reports a repo as configured when it could not read it.

remedy.description: The exact fix when false, e.g. 'restart with --add-dir "D:\work\billing-api"', or '/add-dir D:\work\billing-api' in-session.

trust.description: Per-root harness state that otherwise fails silently at the first /aidlc:sprint launch (the F42 failure mode) — caught here instead.

vcs.description: Version-control state. An unsupported VCS is reported as unsupported and the code is still profiled — never a failed scan and never a silent git assumption.

remotes.description: value: [{name, url}] with credentials stripped from the URL. status=absent means no remote — the signal for git.mode 'local'.

upstream.description: Set when this is a fork: the upstream the project contributes back to. Drives a fork→upstream-PR integration path instead of a push that would fail.

shallow.description: A shallow clone bounds every history-derived fact (commit conventions, branch ages). When true, say so beside those facts.

submodules.description: value: [paths]. Detected and reported; NEVER treated as AIDLC repos, and flagged as a gitlink hazard.

worktrees.description: value: [paths]. Recorded so /aidlc:sprint's worktrees do not collide with the project's own.

lfs.description: LFS in use. Pointer files are never read as source.

enclosingRepo.description: Set when this root is NOT its own repo root but sits INSIDE one — value is the enclosing repo's toplevel path. Detected by requiring `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` to equal the root itself, because `--is-inside-work-tree` searches ancestors and answers true for any folder beneath any repo (a home directory under git makes this true everywhere). Without that check, every VCS fact — branch, remotes, history, size — silently describes the ancestor while citing this root. It is also a real hazard to report: the root's files live in another repo's index, one `git add -A` from being committed there.

languages.description: Detected from manifests, with the paths that carry each. At minimum: TS/JS, Python, Java/Kotlin, C#/.NET, Go, Ruby, PHP, Rust.

ci.description: CI systems in use, with their config paths. Reconciling CI's gate with the local gate is ADOPT-4's job; recording it is this one's.

hooks.description: Pre-existing git hook managers (husky, pre-commit.com, lefthook). Recorded so the AIDLC pre-commit layer does not duplicate them.

migrationTools.description: Migration tooling and its directory (Prisma, TypeORM, Alembic, Flyway, Liquibase, EF Core, Rails, Django, golang-migrate).

containers.description: Container/dev-env requirements (Dockerfile, compose, devcontainer) — the difference between a gate that needs services and one that does not.

entryPoints.description: The commands the project ALREADY has. Detection only: the ordered, executable gate definition is pipeline.gates (ADOPT-4), which reads these. An entry point recorded absent must surface as a coverage hole and must never be counted green.

gates.description: The ORDERED verification sequence proposed for this root's pipeline.gates — the project's real gate, derived from its own entry points, hooks and CI rather than assumed to be npm scripts. Order is part of the contract: the run skill executes it top to bottom. Every entry traces to evidence, and a gate the project does not have is recorded status=absent so it surfaces as a coverage hole instead of being silently replaced by an AIDLC default.

conventions.description: The project's existing git and review conventions, derived from bounded history and host settings. AIDLC's own defaults (conventional commits, {type}/{id}-{slug} branches, one-item-one-PR) apply only where the project has no convention of its own — and are then marked as defaults, never presented as detected. Consumed when rendering rules/git-workflow.md.

branchPattern.description: value: the observed pattern, e.g. '{type}/{id}-{slug}', 'JIRA-123-description', 'feature/JIRA-123'. Derived from recent branch names — say how many were looked at in the evidence.

commitStyle.description: mixed is a real and common answer — say so rather than picking the plurality and imposing it.

mergeStrategy.description: Derived from merge-commit shape in history (a squash-only repo has no merge commits on its default branch) and, where readable, the host's allowed-merge settings.

integrationBranch.description: The branch feature work targets when it is NOT the default branch — GitFlow's `develop`. Load-bearing: the run skill must branch from and integrate into this, not into `main`.

longLivedBranches.description: value: [patterns] such as ['develop', 'release/*', 'hotfix/*']. Distinguishes a branch that must never be deleted or force-updated from a stale feature branch.

hotfixRoute.description: A distinct branch/integration path for production incidents, where the project has one (e.g. hotfix/* cut from a release tag, merged to both main and develop). Recorded so an urgent item is not forced through the normal flow.

codeowners.description: value: {path, entryCount} for a CODEOWNERS file. Record the path and how many rules it holds — the owner identities are already in the repo and need not be copied into the profile.

requiredReviewers.description: Approval count / required reviewer policy, where the host API allows reading it. Unknown offline — say so rather than assuming none.

protectedBranches.description: value: [{branch, requiredChecks[], enforced}] from the host API where readable. status=absent means the API said there is no protection — a repo whose PRs would merge UNGATED, which must be named explicitly. unknown means the API could not be read (offline, or no permission), which is NOT the same as unprotected.

pushAccess.description: fork-only ⇒ the contribution path is fork + upstream PR. Detecting this at adoption time is what stops a run from failing at its first push.

packages.description: The package dimension of a monorepo: one git repo, many independently-owned packages with their own gates and release cadence. Present on a root classified monorepo, which is what lets a workspace hold a monorepo beside single-app repos without a second layout value. Becomes the config's packages[] registry, which routes items exactly as repos[] does — the runnable leaf is still one branch and one PR, now scoped to a package inside one repo.

name.description: The package's own name as its manifest declares it (`@acme/web`, `acme-worker`, the Maven artifactId). Routing and PR labels use it, so it must match what the project calls it — not a folder name invented here.

role.description: One line, derived — used as a routing hint exactly as a repo's role is.

stack.description: Per-package stack, same shape as a repo's: {frontend, backend, databases}. A monorepo's packages routinely differ (a Next.js app beside a Python worker), and resolving stack per repo would hand the worker the web standards.

dependsOn.description: Other packages IN THIS ROOT that this one depends on, by their `name`, read from the manifests (a workspace: protocol dependency, a Maven module dependency, a Cargo path dependency). This is what lets cross-package work sequence the way cross-repo work does: a change to a shared package lands before its consumers. Names must resolve to siblings in this array, and the graph must be acyclic — a cycle makes 'which lands first' unanswerable.

entryPoints.description: Per-package overrides, same shape as the root's entryPoints.

releasable.description: Whether this package versions and publishes on its own cadence (a changeset config listing it, an independent Lerna version, its own publishable manifest). False/absent means it releases with the repo — which /aidlc:release must say plainly rather than cutting a per-package release the tooling cannot support.

releaseTooling.description: value: {tool, independentVersioning} where tool is one of changesets | lerna | nx-release | semantic-release | maven-versions | cargo-release | manual, and independentVersioning says whether packages version separately. This is what decides whether /aidlc:release can cut a PER-PACKAGE release or must say plainly that the repo releases as one unit. status=absent means the repo has no release tooling at all — also an answer, and better stated than assumed.

saas.description: The runtime constraints for this root, when it serves a live product. Absent on a library, a CLI or a docs root — and absence here means the agent briefs carry no runtime constraints, not that the constraints do not exist.

workspaceTooling.description: The monorepo's own tool, when it has one (pnpm workspaces, npm/yarn workspaces, Nx, Turborepo, Lerna, Maven multi-module, Gradle composite, Bazel, Cargo workspace). An affected-graph runner (Nx/Turbo) is load-bearing: it is what lets a per-item gate run affected targets only.

agentConfigs.description: Other AI-agent configuration already in the repo (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules, .github/copilot-instructions.md). Detected so it is REFERENCED rather than duplicated or clobbered.

humanAuthored.description: Best-effort: true means its content must never be overwritten, only merged around.

docs.description: Existing architecture/decision documentation, wherever it lives (docs/adr, RFCs/, a Confluence or Notion link in the README). Linked from the ADR index by ADOPT-10, never copied or relocated.

coverage.description: How thoroughly THIS root was read, when it differs from the workspace-wide budget (a large root sampled while small ones were read fully).
